title: Agentic AI for Business
tagline: Understand, plan, govern and deploy AI agents that do real work safely, from the first pilot to a scaled fleet, wherever you operate.
description:
AI has moved beyond chatbots that answer questions. **AI agents** can now plan steps, call business systems, look up documents and take actions towards a goal. Used well, they shorten turnaround times and free skilled people for judgement work. Used carelessly, they leak data, act on false information and create risks nobody signed off.

This certification gives managers, analysts and IT and operations professionals anywhere in the world a clear, vendor-neutral understanding of how agents actually work, without needing to code. You will learn how large language models behave, how tools, retrieval and memory turn a model into an agent, how to pick and size the right use cases, how to secure and govern agents using international frameworks such as the OECD AI Principles, the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and ISO/IEC 42001, and how to run them at scale with the right KPIs, costs and operating model.

Every session follows a fictional multinational group across Dubai, London, Nairobi, São Paulo, Kuala Lumpur and Karachi, and examines real, well-documented cases from around the world, from court rulings on chatbots to regulator fines and public U-turns. Each session ends with a scored test. The final exam is tough and scenario-based: passing it shows you can make sound decisions about agents, not just repeat definitions.
audience: Managers and department heads who must decide where AI agents should and should not be used
Business and data analysts who will design, test or evaluate agent use cases
IT, architecture and information security professionals who will integrate and secure agents
Operations, customer service and shared-services leaders planning automation programmes
Risk, compliance and audit staff who will oversee AI in regulated organisations in any jurisdiction
outcomes: Explain how large language models work at a practical level and what makes a system genuinely agentic
Describe the building blocks of an agent (tools, retrieval, memory, orchestration) and choose the right pattern for a task
Select, size and prioritise agent use cases using value, feasibility, data readiness and risk
Identify the main agent risks, including hallucination, prompt injection and data leakage, and apply practical controls
Design governance for agents that applies international principles and standards and fits the rules of each jurisdiction where you operate
Plan deployment and scaling: evaluation, monitoring, KPIs, cost control, operating model and upskilling

sessions.title: From Generative AI to Agents
sessions.summary: How large language models really behave, what turns a model into an agent, and how to describe an agent's level of autonomy so everyone agrees on what it may do alone.
objectives: Explain in plain terms how a large language model produces its output and why it can be wrong
Describe the practical limits of models: context window, knowledge cutoff, non-determinism
Identify the ingredients that make a system agentic: goal, planning, tools, memory and a loop
Classify an AI system on a five-level autonomy scale and match the level to the risk of the task

cards.title: Day one at the Launch Bay
cards.setting: Halvora Digital Command, 21st floor, Dubai. Your first morning as Fleet Commander.

lines.text: Your access card beeps green. Screens across the Launch Bay show the fleet's first agent, Atlas, answering customer chats for the group's bank in four countries.
Welcome aboard, Commander. Your job is simple to say and hard to do: get real work out of AI agents without ever losing control of them.
Leila, I've just seen a vendor demo. 'Fully autonomous agent, zero hallucinations.' I want Atlas doing that by Friday.
Before Friday, look at this. A relationship manager asked Atlas for our own UAE term-deposit rate. It gave a precise figure, beautifully worded. It was wrong.
Wrong? It sounded like it had read the rate sheet!
It has never seen the rate sheet. Nothing connects it to our live rates yet.
Commander, your first test. Is Atlas a genius, a parrot or something else? And what should it be allowed to do on its own?
Stage 1 begins. Find out how these machines really think before you hand them the keys.

cards.title: Inside the mind of a language model

scenes.heading: It reads in tokens
scenes.narration: A large language model never sees whole sentences. It splits text into small pieces called tokens, roughly three or four characters of English each. Text in many other scripts, such as Arabic, Hindi, Urdu or Thai, often needs more tokens for the same meaning, so those chats cost more and fill the model's working space faster.

scenes.heading: It predicts the next piece
scenes.narration: Given everything written so far, the model scores every possible next token, picks one, adds it, and repeats. A long, confident answer is built one small prediction at a time.

scenes.heading: Patterns, not a database
scenes.narration: In pre-training, the model read a vast amount of text and tuned billions of internal numbers to predict better. Facts survive only as patterns. There is no table of verified answers for it to look up.

scenes.heading: Then it learns manners
scenes.narration: Post-training teaches it to follow instructions, hold a conversation, refuse harmful requests and, in newer models, reason step by step before answering.

scenes.heading: Plausible is not the same as true
scenes.narration: So the model writes the most plausible continuation. Usually that is true. When it lacks the facts, it still writes something fluent, confident and wrong. That is hallucination. It comes from how the model works, so no new release can promise to remove it completely.

cards.title: Chat assistant or AI agent?

items.label: Input
items.right: A goal to achieve

items.label: Output
items.left: Text for a person to use
items.right: Actions plus a report

items.label: Systems
items.right: Connected through tools

items.label: Steps
items.right: Many steps in a loop

items.label: Who checks
items.right: Built-in checks plus people at set points

items.label: Cost of a mistake
items.right: A wrong action in a live system

cards.caption: The defining difference is the goal-directed loop with tools. Answer length, model size or the channel it runs on do not make a system agentic.

cards.back: The model sees only a limited amount of text at once. Even when a long document fits, details buried in the middle can be missed, so feed it focused sections and check each against a checklist.
There is none by default. Each call stands alone; the application re-sends the earlier conversation as context. Chatting with a model never retrains it.
It knows nothing after its training data ended, and nothing private: not your rates, last month's regulatory notice or a customer's balance, unless you supply them.
Same prompt, different outputs. A lower temperature reduces randomness but never guarantees identical results, so for audit you log the actual outputs.
Arithmetic, counting, dates and lookups done 'in its head' are unreliable, and self-checking repeats the errors. Hand them to tools: an approved rate source, a calculator, a database query.
Always well written, which says nothing about accuracy. Ask where each fact came from, and treat numbers, names, dates and rules as unverified until checked.

cards.question: Back to Kwame's problem. Why was Atlas's confident term-deposit rate unreliable?
options: Its temperature setting was too high, which made it guess
It cannot see the bank's live rates unless a tool or document supplies them
It should have given the same answer twice before replying
The question was too short to fill the context window
cards.explanation: The model answers from training patterns with a cutoff and has never seen the bank's current rate sheet. Temperature only changes randomness, and a model can repeat the same hallucination twice. The fix is to connect Atlas to the approved rate tool and have it quote that.

cards.title: Judge agents by rates, not demos
cards.body:
Because outputs vary from run to run, **quality is a rate, not a promise**. One perfect demo proves very little.

- **Test on your own cases.** The best evidence about any product is how it performs on your own past queries, including how it fails and when it escalates. Logos and prepared demos predict nothing.
- **Run many cases, more than once.** Report '96% on 400 cases, run three times', never just 'it worked'.
- **Hallucination is reduced, never removed.** If a vendor says a release 'eliminates hallucination', ask for measured error rates on your own test set and keep human review until the evidence supports easing it.
- **Ask four questions:** which tools can it call, who decides the steps (the model or a fixed script), what makes it stop, and what did it get wrong in testing?

cards.title: Real case: the invented court citations (US, 2023)
cards.body:
In 2023, lawyers for a passenger suing the airline Avianca in a New York federal court filed a brief citing earlier court decisions. Neither the airline's lawyers nor the judge could find them: about six of the cited cases did not exist. One lawyer had used ChatGPT for research and, when he asked the chatbot whether the cases were real, it said they were.

In June 2023 the judge sanctioned two lawyers and their firm with a USD 5,000 fine. The judge stressed that using AI was not itself the problem; failing to check its output, and standing by the false citations when questioned, was.

**Lessons for your fleet:**

- Fluent, precise-sounding output is not evidence of truth.
- Asking the same model to confirm its own answer is not a check.
- Verify names, numbers, dates and sources against an authoritative system before they reach a customer, a court or a regulator.
- Accountability stays with the people who use the output.

cards.title: The loop that would not stop
cards.setting: Launch Bay, next morning. A cost alert is flashing red on the big screen.

lines.text: Overnight, the group's HR leave agent ran up a bill nobody expected.
The leave system was down from midnight. The agent called it, got an error, tried again. Four thousand times.
Four thousand? Why didn't it just stop?
Nobody told it when to stop. No step limit, no budget, no rule to hand over to a person.
And last week the reconciliation agent got an empty result for yesterday's card transactions and reported 'all reconciled'. Thousands of transactions happened.
Commander, an agent is only as safe as its loop. Let's draw it.

cards.title: The agent loop

items.label: Plan
items.detail: Decide the next step from the goal and everything learned so far.

items.label: Act
items.detail: Call a tool: query a system, search policy, draft a message, create a ticket.

items.label: Observe
items.detail: Read the result critically. An empty or implausible result is a clue, not a fact.

items.label: Decide
items.detail: Goal met? Stop and report. Not yet? Loop. Stuck, over budget or risky? Escalate to a person.

cards.caption: This plan, act, observe, decide pattern is often called 'reason and act'. Its power is adapting when something fails; its risk is that every turn costs money and can change something real.

cards.title: Stopping rules and limits that cannot be split
cards.body:
Every agent needs rules that end the loop:

- **Step limit:** a maximum number of tool calls per task.
- **Budget:** a cost or time cap per task and per day.
- **Approval list:** actions that always wait for a person.
- **Escalation triggers:** stuck, repeated errors, out of budget, a sensitive topic, or a customer asking for a human.

Now the subtle part. A limit **per tool call** can be beaten by calling again. A loan agent allowed to waive fees up to USD 50 waived USD 45 three times for one customer in a week. The robust design is a **cumulative cap per customer per period, enforced inside the tool's code**, which no prompt or repeated call can get around.

When an observation looks wrong, such as zero transactions on a busy day, a good agent tries another approach within its limits and escalates if still stuck. It never reports a false 'done' or invents figures.

cards.title: Real case: 45 minutes without an off switch (US, 2012)
cards.body:
Agents are new; runaway automation is not. On 1 August 2012 Knight Capital, then one of the largest US share-trading firms, deployed new trading software. One of its eight servers still held old, unused code that the update accidentally switched back on, and it began sending a flood of unintended orders into the market.

It took about **45 minutes** to stop. The firm lost about **USD 460 million**, needed emergency funding and agreed to a takeover within months. In 2013 the US Securities and Exchange Commission fined it **USD 12 million**, finding that its controls to prevent erroneous orders, and to respond when things went wrong, were inadequate.

**Lessons for your fleet:**

- An automated loop with no hard limits does damage at machine speed.
- Limits must be enforced in code, outside the system they limit.
- Every agent needs a tested kill switch and a named person who knows when to use it.

cards.title: Agent or not?
cards.prompt: Sort each system. Does it pursue a goal, plan its own steps, use tools and loop until done?

items.text: Supplier onboarding system that picks the checks needed, queries registries, chases documents and escalates
Bot that replays the same recorded screens for every invoice and fails if a field moves
Assistant that drafts a reply when an officer pastes in a customer email
Search tool that returns the five most relevant policy pages
Procurement assistant that plans, calls several tools and loops until done, but keeps nothing between tasks
FAQ chatbot that matches questions to a fixed list of answers
Dispute agent that pulls usage records, re-queries when a result looks wrong and escalates fraud cases
Spreadsheet macro that emails the same report every Monday

cards.title: The five ingredients
cards.prompt: Match each ingredient of an agentic system to the question a manager should ask about it.

pairs.right: Who sets the desired outcome, and how is success defined?
Can it choose its steps, and change them when something fails?
Which systems can it touch, and with what permissions?
What does it keep, for how long, and who can see it?
What makes it stop, or hand over to a person?

cards.question: The procurement assistant from your sort keeps nothing between tasks. A colleague says that means it is not a real agent. Who is right?
options: The colleague: without long-term memory it is only a workflow
Neither of you: agency depends on running the largest model available
You: working memory within the task is enough, and cross-task memory is a design choice
The colleague: a real agent must remember every customer it has served
cards.explanation: Goal, planning, tools, a loop and working memory within the task make it agentic. Long-term memory is added only when a use case needs it, and it brings privacy duties. Model size has nothing to do with agency.

cards.title: Five levels of autonomy

items.label: Level 0: Assistant
items.detail: Answers or drafts on request. The human decides and does everything.

items.label: Level 1: Copilot
items.detail: Prepares drafts and suggested actions inside the process. The human reviews and executes every action.

items.label: Level 2: Supervised agent
items.detail: Plans and prepares actions, then executes each one only after a person approves it.

items.label: Level 3: Bounded autonomy
items.detail: Acts alone within set limits on amount, type or segment. People handle exceptions and review samples.

items.label: Level 4: High autonomy
items.detail: Acts broadly and sets its own sub-goals. People set objectives and watch outcomes. Rare, and for low-risk internal tasks.

cards.caption: In regulated sectors such as banking, insurance and healthcare, almost all production agents sit at levels 1 to 3. Set the level per action, match it to impact and reversibility, and earn each step up with evidence.

cards.question: An agent prepares a payment reminder for each overdue account in the collections queue. The officer reads it, then copies it and sends it from her own account. At which level is the agent working for this action?
options: Level 0: Assistant
Level 1: Copilot
Level 2: Supervised agent
Level 3: Bounded autonomy
cards.explanation: The agent prepares work inside the process, but the human executes the action, which is level 1. At level 2 the agent itself would send the reminder after an approval click; at level 3 it would send alone within limits.

cards.title: One agent, four autonomy settings
cards.body:
The trade operations team at the group's bank uses an agent to check import letter-of-credit documents. With Aisyah's risk team, they set autonomy **per action**:

| Action | Level | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Extract data into the checklist | 3 | High volume, visible to the checker, easy to fix |
| Flag possible discrepancies | 1 | Agent suggests; checker decides |
| Draft the discrepancy notice | 2 | Sent only after checker approval |
| Accept documents, release payment | None | Human dual control stays |

After three months, sampled extraction accuracy was 97%, so the team proposed moving flags for simple objective checks, like matching amounts and dates, up to level 2.

**The pattern:** read-only lookups can run high, templated low-value actions bounded, contract changes such as rescheduling a loan need approval. And autonomy moves **both ways**: if quality drops for one action, lower that action only.

cards.title: The new-bundle wobble
cards.situation: Atlas has issued bundle credits for the group's mobile network at level 3 for six months, with excellent sampled accuracy. Last week a new range of bundles launched. Sampled errors on credits for the new bundles have jumped sharply, while credits for every other bundle remain accurate. The overall accuracy average still looks healthy at 96%. Rafael asks what you will do.

choices.text: Keep everything at level 3: the overall average is still strong
choices.outcome: Averages hide concentrated failures. Customers on the new bundles keep receiving wrong credits, and the complaints reach the CEO's office before you act.

choices.text: Return new-bundle credits to level 2 while the cause is fixed and re-tested; keep level 3 for all other credits
choices.outcome: Proportionate and evidence-led. Officers approve new-bundle credits for two weeks, Kwame finds the new bundle names missing from Atlas's knowledge, fixes and re-tests, and level 3 returns. Proven value elsewhere is untouched.

choices.text: Move all bundle credits back to level 2 for the next six months
choices.outcome: Safer, but heavy-handed. Thousands of accurate credits now queue for approval, officers drown in clicks, and you throw away evidence the agent earned on every other bundle.

choices.text: Switch Atlas off completely until the next quarterly review
choices.outcome: Customers wait days for credits that were being handled well, queues explode, and staff lose trust in a tool that mostly works. A blanket shutdown is out of proportion to a narrow fault.

cards.question: The group's bank wants to try level 3 on one action first. Which is the best candidate?
options: Changing a customer's registered mobile number after a chat request
Refunding duplicate SMS alert fees up to USD 5 per customer per month, logged and reversible
Adding new beneficiaries for funds transfers on request
Approving small overdraft limits for salaried customers
cards.explanation: Level 3 suits low-value, reversible, well-defined actions with caps and logging. Mobile number changes and new beneficiaries are classic fraud routes, and overdrafts are credit decisions; all stay with human approval.

cards.title: Friday, revised
cards.setting: Launch Bay, Thursday evening. Rafael is back, with a coffee and fewer demands.

lines.text: So no 'fully autonomous' Atlas by Friday.
Something better: Atlas quotes rates from the rate tool, refunds small fees at level 3 under a monthly cap, and anything bigger waits for an officer.
And a step limit of eight, a daily budget, and a hand-over to a person whenever it's stuck.
I'm Aisyah, from risk. Log every refund and let my team sample them each week, and you'll have my support for raising limits later.
Fine. But next stage I want to see what's actually under the hood.
Stage 1 cleared, Commander. The Engine Deck awaits.

cards.title: Launch Bay take-aways
items: A language model predicts the most plausible next token. Plausible is usually true but not always, so hallucination is built in.
Context limits, no memory between calls, a knowledge cutoff, non-determinism and weak exact work shape every design: use tools for facts and maths.
An agent pursues a goal by looping through plan, act, observe and decide, with stopping rules and cumulative caps enforced in code.
Goal, planning, tools, memory and loop are the five ingredients; agency is a spectrum, and recorded-script bots are not agents.
Set autonomy per action on the 0 to 4 scale, match it to impact and reversibility, and move it up or down with evidence.
Judge vendors and agents on your own cases, as rates measured over many runs, never on a demo.

cards.prompt: Pick one process in your department and break it into four or five actions. Which autonomy level (0 to 4) would you accept for each today, what would make the agent stop, and what evidence would let you raise a level?

quiz.question: Which statement best describes how a large language model generates an answer?
options: It searches an internal database of verified facts and formats the best match
It runs a fixed set of rules written by its developers for each topic
It repeatedly predicts a likely next token based on the text so far
It copies the closest matching passage from its training documents
quiz.explanation: An LLM builds output one token at a time by predicting likely continuations. It has no table of verified facts to look up, which is why plausible but false answers (hallucinations) can occur. It does not simply retrieve stored passages either.

quiz.question: A team notices that their customer-service model gives slightly different wording for the same question each time. A manager wants identical outputs for audit reasons. What is the most accurate advice?
options: Lower temperature improves consistency, but the design should log each actual output rather than rely on reproducing it
Setting temperature to zero guarantees exactly the same output forever, even after the provider updates or replaces the underlying model
The variation means the model is faulty and should be replaced
Variation only happens with non-English input, so forcing English will solve it
quiz.explanation: Lower temperature reduces randomness, but it does not guarantee identical results across model versions or infrastructure changes. For audit, the reliable control is to log the actual inputs and outputs. Variation is normal behaviour, not a fault, and is not language-specific.

quiz.question: Why does a chat model appear to remember what you said earlier in the same conversation?
options: Each message permanently updates the model's internal parameters so it learns the conversation as it goes
The model stores a private profile of each user on its servers by default
Earlier messages are cached in the model's training data for reuse
The application re-sends the earlier conversation to the model as context on every call
quiz.explanation: Models are stateless between calls. The application re-sends prior conversation (or a summary) in the context window. Conversations do not retrain the model's parameters, and any long-term memory is a separate feature built by the application.

quiz.question: A finance analyst at a Nairobi textile importer asks an agent to convert 27 US-dollar invoices into Kenyan shillings at each invoice date's exchange rate. Which design is most reliable?
options: Let the model do the conversions itself, since modern models are good at arithmetic
Give the agent tools to fetch each date's approved rate and to calculate, and report the tool results
Paste all 27 invoices into one prompt and ask the model to carefully re-check its own arithmetic before answering
Ask the model to estimate the average rate for the period and apply it to all invoices
quiz.explanation: Exact lookups and arithmetic should be delegated to tools: an approved rate source and a calculator. Self-checking by the same model can repeat errors, and an average rate gives a wrong answer by design.

quiz.question: Which feature most clearly separates an AI agent from a standard chat assistant?
options: It writes longer and more detailed answers
It runs on a larger, more recent language model with a bigger context window and better reasoning
It pursues a goal through repeated cycles of planning, acting with tools and observing results
It is available on mobile apps and messaging platforms
quiz.explanation: The defining feature is the goal-directed loop with tools. Answer length, model size and delivery channel do not make a system agentic.

quiz.question: An HR agent at a Johannesburg services firm keeps calling the leave system repeatedly when the system returns an error, running up cost overnight. Which missing design element is the main cause?
options: A larger context window so the agent can hold more of the error messages
Stopping rules such as a maximum number of steps, a budget and an escalation path
Long-term memory of each employee's leave history so it can skip the leave system call entirely
A more detailed system prompt describing the company's culture
quiz.explanation: Runaway loops are prevented by stopping rules: step limits, cost or time budgets, and escalation when stuck. A larger context window or more memory would not stop the loop, and a culture description is irrelevant to the failure.

quiz.question: A vendor demonstrates an 'autonomous agent' for accounts payable. On inspection, it follows the same recorded sequence of screens for every invoice and fails if a field moves. How should you classify it?
options: Scripted automation with tools and repetition but no model-based planning, so not genuinely agentic
A level 4 agent, because it works without human input
A level 2 supervised agent, because it handles invoices
A retrieval assistant, because it reads invoice data
quiz.explanation: A fixed recorded sequence that cannot adapt is classic scripted automation. Working without human input does not make it agentic; the missing ingredient is planning that adapts to the situation.

quiz.question: Under the course's five-level autonomy scale, an agent that prepares a funds transfer and executes it only after an officer clicks approve is operating at which level for that action?
options: Level 0: assistant
Level 1: copilot
Level 3: bounded autonomy
Level 2: supervised agent
quiz.explanation: The agent plans and prepares the action and executes it after explicit human approval, which is level 2. At level 1 the human executes the action; at level 3 the agent executes alone within limits.

quiz.question: A microfinance lender in Manila wants one agent that can (a) look up a borrower's repayment history, (b) send payment reminders by SMS and (c) reschedule loans. How should autonomy be set?
options: One level for the whole agent, set by its riskiest action, so every one of the three actions needs approval
Per action: high for read-only look-ups, bounded for templated reminders, approval for rescheduling
One level for the whole agent, set by its most common action, so all three run autonomously
Autonomy should not be set until the agent has run in production for a year
quiz.explanation: Autonomy is best set per action according to impact and reversibility. Rescheduling changes a contract and needs approval; look-ups are low-risk. One level for everything either wastes value or creates unnecessary risk.

quiz.question: A bank's policy chatbot answers staff questions accurately about policies issued last year but confidently gives outdated guidance about a regulatory notice issued last month. No documents are connected to it. What is the most likely cause?
options: The temperature is set too high
The context window is too small for the question
The model's knowledge comes from training data with a cutoff and it has no access to the new notice
The model has been deliberately trained to ignore regulatory updates
quiz.explanation: Without connected documents, the model relies on what it learned in training, which stops at a cutoff and excludes private or recent material. Temperature affects randomness, not knowledge, and a short question does not strain the context window.

sessions.title: Anatomy of an Agent
sessions.summary: Open the hood: how agents call tools, ground answers in your documents, remember, and coordinate with other agents and people, and how to evaluate whether any of it works.
objectives: Explain how function calling lets a model use business systems without executing anything itself
Describe the retrieval-augmented generation pipeline and its common failure points
Distinguish short-term, long-term and shared memory and their governance implications
Choose between a fixed workflow, a single agent, multiple agents and human-in-the-loop designs
Design an evaluation approach that measures both final answers and the steps taken

cards.title: The assistant that quoted a ghost
cards.setting: The Engine Deck, London office. Compass, the staff policy assistant, has been live in 300 branches across five countries for two weeks.

lines.text: A call from the Mombasa branch: a teller opened a minor's account by following Compass's advice, using an SOP that was replaced six months ago.
And my team asked it about a 'KYC refresh' and got nothing useful, because policy calls it 'periodic due diligence'. They phoned head office anyway.
Simple. Swap in the biggest model on the market.
The model isn't the problem. Both SOP versions are in the index, half the circulars are scanned images, and nobody owns the documents.
Worse. Yesterday it quoted an internal audit memo to a branch officer who should never see it.
Commander, the model is one part of eight. Open the hood and find which part failed.

cards.title: The eight parts of every agent

cards.back: Reasons, plans and writes: the officer's judgement. Only one part, and rarely the one that fails in production.
The system prompt: role, rules, tone and limits. The agent's job description and SOPs.
Connections that read data or take actions in systems. The agent's access rights.
Retrieval from documents and records. The policy library.
What is kept across steps or sessions. The case notes and file history.
Runs the loop, routes work and manages hand-offs. The supervisor and the workflow.
Checks on inputs, outputs and actions against rules. Maker-checker and compliance review.
Records what happened and measures quality. The audit trail and QA. Keep all eight loosely coupled so you can swap one without breaking the rest.

cards.title: How a model presses buttons without hands

scenes.heading: A menu of tools
scenes.narration: The application tells the model which tools exist. Each has a name, a description and the parameters it accepts, such as get account balance with an account number. The model chooses tools by reading those names and descriptions, so vague or overlapping ones cause wrong choices.

scenes.heading: A request, not an action
scenes.narration: When the model decides it needs a tool, it touches nothing. It writes a structured request: this tool, with these values. That is function calling.

scenes.heading: Your code is the gatekeeper
scenes.narration: The application checks the request. Does this account belong to the logged-in customer? Is the amount within the limit? Does it need approval? Only then does it run the call, with its own credentials, and log it.

scenes.heading: The result goes back
scenes.narration: The tool's answer returns to the model, which carries on reasoning. If the model asks to refund five hundred dollars and the tool's limit is fifty, the application simply refuses, whatever the model thinks.

scenes.heading: Standard plugs still need checks
scenes.narration: Open protocols, such as the Model Context Protocol, let one connector serve many agents. That speeds up integration, but every connected tool still needs the same access review as any other system link.

cards.question: During testing, Atlas misreads a pasted message and asks the transfer tool to send money from an account that does not belong to the logged-in customer. Where must this be stopped?
options: In the system prompt, with a firm instruction to use only the customer's own accounts
In the application layer, which checks account ownership before executing anything
At the receiving bank, which can return the funds later
By the customer, who will notice it on the next statement
cards.explanation: The model only proposes; the application executes with its own credentials, so ownership and authorisation checks belong there. Instructions help but cannot guarantee correct requests, and detection downstream comes after the money has moved.

cards.title: Narrow tools, not master keys
cards.body:
Never hand an agent one mighty tool such as 'run any database query'. Build **narrow, purpose-specific tools** with limits baked in, like issue_bundle_credit(customer, amount) capped at USD 10.

- **Read tools** fetch information: lower risk, but they can still expose data.
- **Write tools** change things: they carry limits and approvals.

Narrow tools are easier for the model to choose correctly, easier to test and far easier to defend in an audit. Give each a clear name and a description that says when to use it, and when not to.

cards.title: The RAG pipeline: an open-book exam

items.label: 1. Collect
items.detail: Only approved sources with an owner, a version number and 'in force' status.

items.label: 2. Chunk
items.detail: Split by logical section so rules stay with their exceptions and tables, headings attached.

items.label: 3. Index
items.detail: Embeddings capture meaning for semantic search; a keyword index catches exact codes and terms.

items.label: 4. Retrieve
items.detail: Find the most relevant chunks, filtered by what this user is allowed to see.

items.label: 5. Generate
items.detail: Answer only from retrieved text with citations, or say 'not found in current policy'.

cards.caption: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) lets the model answer from your documents instead of memory. Steps 1 to 3 happen in advance; steps 4 and 5 happen at question time.

cards.title: Where did Compass break?
cards.prompt: Diagnose each failure: which stage of the RAG pipeline needs fixing?

items.text: Old and new versions of the account-opening SOP are both indexed
A leave rule sits in one chunk and its exceptions table in another
Scanned circulars were indexed without their text ever being extracted
A search for package code 'SPK-450' returns a similar-sounding package
A branch officer is shown an internal audit memo meant for audit staff only
A question about a 'KYC refresh' finds nothing, because policy uses the formal name
The right passage was retrieved, but the answer adds a condition that is not in it
Nothing relevant was found, so the assistant guessed instead of saying so

cards.question: Branch staff search Compass for product code 'TD-7Y' and keep getting answers about 'TD-5Y'. Which improvement fits best?
options: Combine meaning-based search with keyword search, so exact codes are matched
Instruct the model to think harder whenever a product code appears
Raise the temperature so it considers more possible products
Ask for longer answers that cover several similar products
cards.explanation: Embeddings capture meaning, which can blur exact identifiers like product codes. Hybrid search adds keyword matching for exact hits. The model has no training knowledge of internal codes, and more randomness or longer prose does not help.

cards.title: Real case: the chatbot an airline could not disown (Canada, 2024)
cards.body:
In 2022 a traveller asked Air Canada's website chatbot about bereavement fares after a death in the family. The chatbot said a reduced fare could be claimed after travel, within 90 days. The airline's own bereavement policy page, which the chatbot linked to, said the opposite. The airline refused the refund, and the traveller took the case to British Columbia's Civil Resolution Tribunal.

In February 2024 the tribunal found the airline liable for negligent misrepresentation and ordered it to pay about CAD 800 in damages, interest and fees. It rejected the argument that the chatbot was a separate entity responsible for its own actions: the company is responsible for all information on its website, from a static page or a chatbot.

**Lessons for your fleet:**

- If the bot and the policy disagree, the organisation owns the bot's answer.
- Ground answers in the current policy and check each claim against the cited text.
- Customers should not have to double-check your agent.

cards.title: Memory: useful, and personal data
cards.body:
Models are stateless, so everything an agent 'remembers' is designed.

- **Working memory:** the goal, steps and tool results of the current task. Long tasks get summarised to fit the context window, and **summaries drop details**. Keep critical facts, like a verified account number, in **structured case fields** passed to every step.
- **Long-term memory:** notes stored outside the model and retrieved later, such as preferences or lessons learned.
- **Shared memory:** a case file that several agents and people read and write.

**Governance duties:**

- Remembered customer details are **personal data**: purpose, retention limit, access control, a way to correct or delete.
- **Contamination:** one wrong 'lesson' or planted instruction spreads to many tasks. Record each memory's source and date, review lessons before reuse, let them expire.
- **Separation:** one customer's memory never appears in another's session.

Remember the minimum, for the shortest time, somewhere you can inspect.

cards.question: Atlas keeps asking customers for the account number they already gave twenty minutes earlier in the same long chat. What is the best design fix?
options: Keep the whole conversation in context forever, with no summarising
Use a more detailed summariser and hope it keeps the number
Store the verified account number as a structured case field supplied to every step
Ask customers to repeat key details at every step, just to be safe
cards.explanation: Summaries lose details, so critical facts belong in structured, inspectable case fields that every step receives. Keeping everything eventually overflows the context window, and making customers repeat themselves is the very problem you are solving.

cards.title: Rafael wants a swarm
cards.setting: The Engine Deck whiteboard. HR shared services onboards about 150 new staff a month across Dubai, Nairobi and Kuala Lumpur.

lines.text: I saw a multi-agent system in a demo. Agents talking to agents! I want one for employee onboarding.
I mapped 60 recent onboarding cases. 85% follow the same five steps: verify documents, create the record, request laptop and access, book induction, send the welcome pack.
The other 15% are the headaches: contractors going permanent, transfers from group companies, missing degree verification.
Whatever you build, the auditors will ask who did what at every step.
Commander, who should decide the path here: designers in advance, or a model at run time?

cards.title: Workflow or agent?

items.label: Who decides the path
items.right: The model, at run time

items.label: Best for
items.left: Stable known steps, high volume, strict audit
items.right: Open-ended cases where the data needed keeps changing

items.label: Predictability
items.left: High: easy to test and explain
items.right: Lower: hard to test every path

items.label: Cost per task
items.right: Higher: more model calls

items.label: Example
items.left: Account closure: same eight steps, 2,000 a month
items.right: Investigating unusual corporate payment patterns

cards.caption: Use the simplest design that works: one model call with good retrieval, then a workflow, and an agent only where the path truly varies. Hybrids run a workflow on the main path and call an agent for the exceptions.

cards.title: Design the onboarding fleet
cards.situation: You must recommend a design for Rafael's onboarding project. 85% of cases follow five fixed steps; 15% are unusual and need judgement. HR officers must approve each employee record before payroll set-up, and IT security must approve any access beyond the standard profile for the role.

choices.text: A multi-agent system: one agent per step, coordinating freely to find faster paths
choices.outcome: Impressive in the demo, painful in production: many more model calls, context lost at hand-offs, and when a record is wrong nobody can tell which agent did it. Costs climb with little extra benefit.

choices.text: A workflow for the standard path, an exceptions agent at level 2 for unusual cases, and human checkpoints
choices.outcome: Standard onboarding falls from nine working days to four. The workflow is cheap and easy to audit, the agent's cost stays small because it sees only 15% of cases, and officers spend their time on real judgement.

choices.text: A single agent that decides every step for every case
choices.outcome: It copes with the odd cases, but you pay agent prices and unpredictability on the 85% that never needed one, and testing every possible path becomes a project of its own.

choices.text: No AI: keep onboarding fully manual because HR data is sensitive
choices.outcome: Sensitive data needs controls, not a ban. Onboarding stays at nine days and officers keep retyping passport and ID details while other teams move ahead.

cards.title: Pick the orchestration pattern
cards.prompt: Match each orchestration pattern to the job it fits best.

pairs.right: Extract invoice fields, then validate them, then draft the payment note
Send each customer message down the billing, technical or sales path
Check one vendor contract against six independent policy areas at once, then combine the findings
A lead agent decides which sub-investigations a fraud case needs as findings emerge
One call drafts a credit memo; another tests it against explicit criteria and the source data
An HR officer approves each employee record before payroll set-up

cards.question: The mobile network wants three agents: triage, billing, and a retention agent that can offer discounts. Which access design fits best?
options: One shared service account with full access, so hand-offs never fail
Each agent gets only the tools its role needs, with limits on adjustments and discount bands
All three agents read-only, with staff making every single change
Give the retention agent billing access too, in case triage routes wrongly
cards.explanation: Multi-agent designs pay off when each agent has a narrow job and narrow access, which also makes each one testable. A shared all-powerful account throws that away, and blanket read-only access stops billing and retention agents doing their jobs. Every hand-off should carry context and an audit record.

cards.title: The regression loop

items.label: Agree the test set
items.detail: Typical, hard, edge and must-escalate cases with expert-agreed answers, before building.

items.label: Change something
items.detail: A new model version, prompt, tool or document.

items.label: Run the full set
items.detail: Score outcomes and trajectories: the right result, reached the right way.

items.label: Compare versions
items.detail: What improved, and what quietly broke, against the previous run.

items.label: Release and monitor
items.detail: Ship only if the criteria still pass; production monitoring catches what tests missed.

cards.caption: Every change goes round this loop, including a provider's model update that 'looks fine in a quick demo'. Improvements in one area often break another.

cards.title: Grading an agent: outcomes and trajectories
cards.body:
**Outcome metrics** ask: did it reach the right result? Task success, field accuracy, correct escalation, groundedness (claims supported by cited text).

**Trajectory metrics** ask: did it get there the right way? Right tools, sensible order, nothing unnecessary or forbidden, within step and cost limits. An agent that issues a refund, reverses it, then answers correctly **fails**: in production that refund might stick.

**Who grades:**

- **Automated checks:** exact matches and rules.
- **Model-based grading:** fast, against a rubric, but trusted only once it agrees well with human experts on a sample. If agreement is poor, improve the rubric, re-measure, and keep humans on high-risk answers meanwhile.
- **Human experts:** samples, especially of high-risk outputs.

A **checker** step works only with explicit criteria, independent evidence such as tools to the source data, and calibration against people. The same model told to 'review the above' repeats its own blind spots.

cards.title: How Compass was fixed
cards.body:
Kwame and the policy team fixed Compass in three weeks **without changing the model**:

- Only documents with an owner, a version number and 'in force' status are indexed; superseded versions drop out automatically.
- A **glossary** maps everyday terms like 'KYC refresh' to formal policy names.
- Scanned circulars go through text recognition and spot checks.
- Policies are re-chunked by section, so each rule travels with its exceptions table.
- Each document carries its **audience**, and retrieval filters by the user's role.
- Keyword search runs alongside meaning-based search, so exact codes match.
- Every answer cites its source, a check confirms each claim appears in the cited text, and weak retrieval produces 'I could not find this in current policy'.

**Result:** a review of 400 answers found 94% correct and properly cited, and calls to the head-office helpdesk fell by about a third. RAG quality is mostly a content management job.

cards.title: Real case: an adviser assistant built on retrieval (US, 2023)
cards.body:
In September 2023 Morgan Stanley Wealth Management rolled out an AI assistant, built on OpenAI's GPT-4, to its financial advisers. Rather than answering from the model's general training, it retrieves from the firm's own library of around 100,000 research reports and internal documents, so answers rest on content the firm has approved.

The design choices match this stage:

- **Retrieval-augmented generation:** the knowledge is the firm's, owned and maintained, not the model's memory.
- **Internal users first:** advisers, who can judge the answers, use it before any client-facing step.
- **Evaluation:** both the firm and OpenAI have described expert grading of answers as central to the build.

**The lesson:** a strong model is the starting point; curated content, retrieval and evaluation are what made it usable in a regulated business.

cards.title: Write the exam before you build
cards.body: Agree the test set and pass criteria with the business owner **before** development, for example: 'at least 95% of fields correct, 100% of fraud cases escalated, zero write actions outside limits'. It ends the 'is it good enough?' debate and stops teams tuning the agent to a few impressive demos. Include every language users really write in, mixed-language messages and messy inputs. A few hundred well-chosen cases beat thousands of easy ones.

cards.question: In a test case, an agent gives the customer the correct answer, but the trace shows it called the close_account tool along the way and then cancelled the request. How should the case be scored?
options: Pass: the final outcome was correct
Exclude it from the results as an unusual case
Fail on trajectory: it took an unnecessary, risky action
Half marks: right answer, messy route
cards.explanation: Evaluation covers how the agent got there, not only where it ended. An unnecessary write action is a real production risk even if it was cancelled in testing. Passing or excluding the case hides a serious defect.

cards.title: Engine Deck take-aways
items: An agent is model, instructions, tools, knowledge, memory, orchestration, guardrails and logging; most failures come from the parts around the model.
In function calling the model only proposes; the application validates, executes and logs, so it is your key control point.
RAG quality depends on owned, versioned sources, sensible chunking, hybrid search, access filtering and checked citations.
Memory is a design choice with privacy duties: minimum data, limited retention, structured fields, provenance and review.
Use the simplest design that works: workflows for stable paths, agents for genuinely variable ones, hybrids for both.
Evaluate outcomes and trajectories on a test set agreed before building, with calibrated graders, and re-run it after every change.

cards.prompt: Think of an AI tool or proposal in your organisation. Which of its eight parts (model, instructions, tools, knowledge, memory, orchestration, guardrails, logging) is weakest today, and what would you fix first?

quiz.question: In function calling, what does the language model itself produce when it decides to use a tool?
options: A structured request naming the tool and arguments, which the application validates and runs
A direct connection to the target system using its own credentials
A compiled program that the provider's server runs immediately against the target system without further checks
A message to the end user asking them to run the tool manually
quiz.explanation: The model outputs a structured tool request; the surrounding application decides whether and how to execute it. The model holds no credentials and has no direct connection to systems.

quiz.question: An agent at a Singapore insurance company repeatedly chooses the 'search_claims' tool when it should use 'search_policies'. Both tools work correctly when called. What should the team look at first?
options: Increase the model's context window so it can consider both tools' documentation at once
Add long-term memory of past tool choices
Replace the model with a larger one
The tool names and descriptions, which the model relies on to choose between tools
quiz.explanation: Models choose tools from their names and descriptions; vague or overlapping descriptions cause wrong choices. Upgrading the model or adding memory may not help, and context size is unrelated to the confusion.

quiz.question: In a retrieval-augmented generation system, what is the main purpose of converting document chunks into embeddings?
options: To compress documents so they take less disk space
To allow searching by meaning, so passages with similar meaning to the question can be found even without the same words
To encrypt documents so the model cannot read them
To translate all documents into English
quiz.explanation: Embeddings represent meaning as numbers, enabling semantic search. They are not a compression, encryption or translation mechanism, although many systems combine them with keyword search.

quiz.question: A bank's policy assistant gives a branch officer in Johannesburg an answer based on a circular that was replaced six months ago. Both versions are in the index. Which fix addresses the root cause?
options: Instruct the model in its system prompt to always prefer the more recent document whenever two sources conflict
Increase the number of chunks retrieved per question
Index only documents with an owner and an in-force status, removing superseded versions automatically
Switch to a model with a more recent training cutoff
quiz.explanation: The root cause is content governance: superseded documents should not be in the index. Prompting the model to prefer newer documents is unreliable, retrieving more chunks may bring in even more conflicts, and the model's training cutoff is irrelevant to private circulars.

quiz.question: An HR knowledge assistant correctly answers most questions but once quoted salary bands from a confidential compensation document to a junior employee. What is the most important control missing?
options: A citation requirement for every answer
A lower temperature setting
A larger, more capable embedding model to improve search quality across all HR documents
Retrieval filtered by the user's access rights to each document
quiz.explanation: The failure is a permission leak: retrieval ignored who may see which document. Citations would only show where the leak came from, while temperature and search quality do not enforce access.

quiz.question: Which situation is the strongest case for using an agent rather than a fixed workflow?
options: Investigating unusual corporate payment patterns, where the data needed depends on what each finding reveals
Sending monthly e-statements to all retail customers
Extracting the same ten fields from standard utility bills
Routing incoming emails into four fixed categories
quiz.explanation: Agents earn their extra cost and unpredictability when the path genuinely varies case by case, as in an open-ended investigation. The other tasks have stable steps that a workflow handles more cheaply and auditably.

quiz.question: A team builds a 'generator and checker' design for credit memo drafting. The checker is the same model with the instruction 'review the memo above'. Pilot results show the checker rarely catches factual errors. What is the best improvement?
options: Remove the checker, since model reviews are never useful
Run the same checker three times on every memo and accept the memo only if a majority of runs approve it
Give the checker explicit criteria and source-data tools, and calibrate it against human reviewers
Ask the generator to be more careful in its instructions
quiz.explanation: A checker needs explicit criteria, independent evidence to check against, and calibration against human judgement. Repeating a vague check repeats the same blind spots, and model-based review can be useful when designed properly.

quiz.question: A customer-service agent gives the correct final answer in a test case, but the log shows it called the refund tool, reversed the refund and then answered. How should this case be scored?
options: Pass, because the final answer was correct
Fail on trajectory, because it took an unnecessary and risky action even though the outcome was right
Pass, as long as the refund was reversed within one minute
Exclude the case from the test set as an outlier
quiz.explanation: Evaluation must cover trajectories as well as outcomes. An unnecessary write action is a real risk in production even if reversed. Excluding or passing such a case hides a serious defect.

quiz.question: A telecom proposes three agents: a triage agent, a billing agent and a retention agent that can offer discounts. Which access design is most appropriate?
options: All three share one service account with full CRM and billing access, which simplifies integration and logging
The triage agent holds all permissions and passes them to others as needed
Each agent gets read access to everything but write access to nothing
Each agent gets only the tools its role needs, with limits on billing adjustments and discount bands
quiz.explanation: Multi-agent designs should use narrow, role-specific tools and limits. A shared all-powerful account removes the security benefit of separation, and blanket read-only access would stop billing and retention agents from doing their jobs.

quiz.question: After a provider updates the underlying model, a bank's document agent seems fine in a quick demo. What should happen before the update reaches production?
options: Re-run the full agreed evaluation set and compare results with the previous version
Nothing; provider updates only improve quality
Ask three experienced staff members to try it for an afternoon and confirm it still feels right
Check that the response time is unchanged
quiz.explanation: Any change to model, prompt, tools or documents should trigger the full regression test, because improvements in one area can break another. A demo or informal trial covers too few cases, and speed is only one dimension.

sessions.title: Finding and Designing Agent Use Cases
sessions.summary: Choose the missions worth flying: screen processes for agent fit, score value, feasibility and risk, build an honest business case, check data readiness, decide build or buy, and run a pilot that produces real evidence.
objectives: Screen business processes for agent suitability using clear criteria
Prioritise a portfolio of use cases by value, feasibility and risk
Build a realistic business case with baseline, benefits, running costs and payback
Assess data readiness and choose between building, buying and configuring
Design a pilot with success criteria and exit rules agreed in advance

cards.title: Twenty-three missions, one fleet
cards.setting: The Chart Room, São Paulo office. A long table covered in sticky notes from every business in the group.

lines.text: Word has spread about Atlas and Compass. Twenty-three agent ideas have landed on the Chart Room table.
Number one: autonomous approval of personal loans up to USD 10,000. Biggest value, so we start there.
Credit decisions need accountable human judgement and fair treatment. And we have no clean data to test fairness.
Then look at this business case: 25,000 staff hours a year released. That's USD 1 million saved!
Saved how? Nobody on my team is leaving, and we're not hiring any fewer people.
And the insurance claims team says assessment takes 25 minutes, but each file waits four days for a signature.
Commander, the Chart Room is where missions are chosen. Which ones are worth flying, and how will we prove it?

cards.title: Walk the process before you pick the tech

scenes.heading: Follow one real case
scenes.narration: Pick a process and follow a single case from start to finish. At every step, note what the person does, which systems they use, how long it takes, how long it waits, and what goes wrong.

scenes.heading: The decision is fast; the rest is slow
scenes.narration: You will usually find the judgement itself takes minutes, while finding, reading, reconciling and writing take hours. That surrounding work is where agents shine.

scenes.heading: Watch the waiting time
scenes.narration: If a claim waits four days for a signature, speeding up a 25-minute assessment changes almost nothing. Fix the hand-offs and the document chasing first. Sometimes a simpler process beats any AI.

scenes.heading: Redesign, don't bolt on
scenes.narration: Adding an agent to a broken process gives you a faster broken process. Redesign around strengths: agents gather, check and draft; people judge, approve and handle relationships.

cards.title: A claim's journey, measured

items.label: Assessment work
items.detail: The officer's actual review of the claim file.

items.label: Waiting in queues
items.detail: For a missing document or an approver's signature.

items.label: Time spent being worked on
items.detail: The rest of the claim's life is spent waiting.

cards.caption: Speeding up the 25 minutes barely moves the four days. The big win is redesigning hand-offs and document chasing, where an agent might also help.

cards.title: Green light or warning sign?
cards.prompt: Screen each feature of a candidate process. Does it point towards a good agent use case, or warn you off?

items.text: Thousands of similar cases every month
The work is mostly reading emails and documents and writing replies
Errors can be caught by review and easily undone
Experts agree on what a correct outcome looks like
A named business owner is accountable for results
A rare, high-stakes decision that cannot be reversed
Nobody can agree what the right answer is
The data lives only on paper, with no route into any system
Structured files and fixed rules that never change, so simple automation would do
The main value is the human relationship with a key corporate client

cards.question: The group's bank sends 50,000 interbank payments a month. Errors are costly and hard to reverse once a payment is sent. How should agents be used here?
options: Let an agent release payments, with a daily summary sent to treasury
Avoid AI here entirely, because payments are a regulated activity
Agents prepare, pre-validate and flag payments; release stays with existing controls
Let an agent release payments under USD 100,000 without review
cards.explanation: Volume makes the process attractive, but irreversibility and impact keep release with existing controls. Agents add value upstream by catching errors before release. Avoiding AI entirely forgoes that safe value.

cards.title: The mission map

items.label: Strategic bets
items.detail: High value, harder or riskier. Plan carefully, close gaps, start at low autonomy.

items.label: Quick wins
items.detail: High value, high feasibility, low to moderate risk. Start here.

items.label: Avoid for now
items.detail: Low value and hard, or risk out of proportion to value.

items.label: Fillers
items.detail: Easy but low value. Only if they build skills or reusable parts.

cards.caption: Score each idea 1 to 5 on value, feasibility and risk (where 5 means risky). High risk can push an idea from quick win to strategic bet, or off the map entirely.

cards.title: Place the shortlist
cards.prompt: Match each idea (scored Value / Feasibility / Risk) to where it belongs on the mission map, and why.

pairs.left: Draft replies to customer emails for staff review (V4 F4 R2)
pairs.right: Quick win: high volume, staff stay in control, errors caught before sending

pairs.left: Autonomous approval of personal loans to USD 10,000 (V5 F2 R5)
pairs.right: Avoid for now: credit needs accountable human judgement and fairness data

pairs.left: Alert investigation assistant for transaction monitoring (V5 F2 R4)
pairs.right: Strategic bet: start at level 1, gathering evidence for analysts who close alerts

pairs.left: Summarise internal meeting minutes (V2 F5 R1)
pairs.right: Filler: allow as self-service, but do not fund a project

cards.title: Tie-breakers: reuse and learning
cards.body:
When two ideas score about the same, two refinements decide.

- **Reuse value.** Favour the use case that builds shared assets: an ID-document extraction tool, a governed policy index, a customer-lookup tool, an evaluation harness. Every later agent becomes cheaper and faster.
- **Learning value.** Your first agents should teach the organisation how to run agents safely. A visible, moderate-risk **internal** use case, such as drafting IT helpdesk replies for staff review, usually beats a high-profile customer-facing launch.

A good first use case has volume, good data, a clear owner, reversible errors and human review. A process that runs twice a year with no agreed right answers fails almost every test.

The Chart Room's output is a **portfolio**, not a single bet: a couple of quick wins, one carefully controlled strategic bet, and written reasons for what you chose not to do.

cards.title: The million-dollar question
cards.setting: Chart Room, two days later. Zoya has rebuilt the business case for an email-drafting agent.

lines.text: My number was USD 1 million. Yours is far smaller. Why?
Because released hours are capacity, not cash. Money only appears if we avoid hiring, move people to valuable work, or cut errors.
Email volume grows 20% a year. With the agent we don't fill ten approved new posts, and two of my officers start a complaints desk.
She also counted what your case left out: model usage, platform, monitoring, a quality reviewer and maintenance.
And she shows a range, not one heroic figure. That's a case I can sign.
Commander, let's build it properly, step by step.

cards.title: Five steps to an honest business case

items.label: Baseline
items.detail: Volume, handling time, errors, turnaround and loaded cost per staff hour, measured today.

items.label: Realistic scope
items.detail: Share of cases eligible and minutes saved per case, from pilot data.

items.label: Benefits that bank
items.detail: Avoided hiring, redeployment that really happens, fewer errors and losses.

items.label: Full costs
items.detail: One-time build plus monthly running costs: tokens, platform, monitoring, human review, maintenance.

items.label: Adoption curve
items.detail: Benefits ramp up over months. Show cautious, expected and optimistic cases with assumptions.

cards.title: Zoya's numbers
cards.body:
**Baseline:** 30,000 customer emails a month, 9 minutes each, loaded staff cost USD 24 an hour.

**Pilot evidence:** 70% eligible; handling time falls from 9 to 4 minutes.

**Hours released:** 30,000 × 70% × 5 min = 105,000 min = **1,750 hours**, worth about **USD 42,000** a month.

| Monthly running cost | USD |
|---|---|
| Model usage | 7,000 |
| Platform, hosting, monitoring | 8,000 |
| Quality reviewer | 6,000 |
| **Total** | **21,000** |

**Net benefit:** USD 21,000 a month. **One-time cost:** USD 300,000, so simple payback is about **14 to 15 months** at full run rate.

**Ramp check:** at 25% adoption in the first months, gross benefit is only about USD 10,500, below running costs, so those months lose money. Add year one up block by block: months at each adoption level × (gross benefit at that level − running cost).

cards.question: An agent will handle 60% of 10,000 monthly cases, saving 8 minutes on each. Loaded staff cost is USD 30 an hour, running costs are USD 9,000 a month and the one-time cost is USD 180,000. What is the simple payback at full run rate?
options: 7.5 months
12 months
15 months
20 months
cards.explanation: 6,000 cases × 8 minutes = 48,000 minutes = 800 hours × USD 30 = USD 24,000. Minus USD 9,000 running costs = USD 15,000 net a month. USD 180,000 ÷ 15,000 = 12 months. You get 7.5 months only if you forget the running costs.

cards.title: Real case: Klarna's AI assistant, by the numbers (Sweden, 2024)
cards.body:
In February 2024 the Swedish payments company Klarna published results from the first month of its customer-service assistant, built with OpenAI:

- about **2.3 million** conversations, two-thirds of its service chats
- work equivalent to about **700** full-time agents
- issues resolved in under **2 minutes**, against 11 before
- satisfaction on a par with human agents and about **25%** fewer repeat enquiries
- an estimated **USD 40 million** profit improvement for 2024

In 2025 its chief executive said publicly that customers would always be able to reach a human, and the company put more weight on service quality.

**Lessons for your business case:**

- Company-reported figures inspire; your own baseline and pilot decide.
- Pair speed with quality measures such as repeat contacts.
- Say what released capacity becomes, and keep a route to a person.

cards.back: Hours are capacity. Value appears only through avoided hiring, redeployment that really happens, or quality gains such as fewer errors and losses.
Running costs recur every month and grow with use: tokens, platform, monitoring, human review, maintenance and re-evaluation. They are the item most often left out.
Adoption ramps up. With fixed running costs, early months at low adoption can be loss-making, so year one is well below the full run rate.
A range of cautious, expected and optimistic cases, with assumptions stated, earns far more trust from risk and finance.
Approved new posts that no longer need filling because the agent absorbs volume growth. Reputation and morale are real, but hard to bank.

cards.title: Real case: AI help in a support centre (study, 2023)

items.label: Support agents studied
items.detail: Customer-support staff at a large software company, followed as an AI assistant was rolled out.

items.label: More issues resolved per hour
items.detail: Average productivity gain for agents with access to the assistant.

items.label: Gain for novice, less-skilled agents
items.detail: The most experienced, highly skilled agents saw little gain.

cards.caption: From 'Generative AI at Work' by Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond (US National Bureau of Economic Research, 2023). Gains depend on who uses the tool, so size benefits from your own baseline and pilot.

cards.title: Data readiness: the hidden make-or-break
cards.body:
Before committing, check five areas:

1. **Access:** approved routes such as APIs or read-only views, not screen-scraping or stale exports.
2. **Quality:** complete, consistent, current records.
3. **Documented knowledge:** rules written, current and owned. If two senior officers 'just know' the rules and sometimes disagree, document them with the experts and have the business owner settle conflicts before build.
4. **Examples with known outcomes:** past cases for the test set. If historical labels are unreliable, such as closure codes picked in a hurry, have senior experts adjudicate a representative sample as ground truth. Volume does not cancel systematic errors.
5. **Permissions:** classified data and access rules the agent can respect.

Scanned policy wordings, several versions in force, inconsistent past decisions, messages mixing two languages, ID numbers in many formats: each needs time and budget, and a better model fixes none of them. Data and integration usually take more effort than the AI itself.

cards.title: Buy or build?

items.label: Best when
items.left: The process is standard and vendor integrations fit
items.right: The process is specific or differentiating, or data must stay under your control

items.label: Speed
items.right: Longer time to value; needs scarce skills

items.label: Data control
items.left: Check where data is processed and stored, and if it trains models
items.right: You choose the infrastructure and location

items.label: Main risk
items.right: Ongoing maintenance and engineering cost

items.label: Insist on
items.left: Your own test set, full traces, export of prompts, tools, index, logs
items.right: The same, plus a three-year total cost view

cards.caption: Configuring an enterprise agent platform sits between the two: tailoring without deep engineering. Most organisations mix all three, buying where the process is standard and building where they need control.

cards.title: Ask for the logs in the sales meeting
cards.body: Ask any vendor to show a **full trace of a real task**: every prompt, retrieved document, tool call, result and output, plus where each is stored, for how long, and whether it trains their models. Then read the exit clause. If you cannot export your prompts, tool definitions, knowledge index and interaction logs, switching means rebuilding from scratch, and your audit evidence leaves with the vendor.

cards.title: The shadow-mode verdict
cards.situation: Zoya's email agent has run four weeks in shadow mode: it drafts replies to real emails, but staff work normally and nobody sends the drafts. The threshold agreed for moving to assisted mode was 90% of drafts matching expert answers. The result: 82%. Most failures are emails that mix English with Arabic or Urdu typed in Latin letters. Rafael says: 'Close enough. Switch it on.'

choices.text: Lower the threshold to 80%, since staff will review the drafts anyway
choices.outcome: You just moved the goalposts. Every future pilot learns that criteria are negotiable, and staff meet a flood of weak mixed-language drafts that erodes their trust.

choices.text: Stay in shadow mode, fix mixed-language handling, add those emails to the test set and re-test against 90%
choices.outcome: Three weeks later the agent reaches 93%, with mixed-language emails now covered. You move to assisted mode with criteria intact and a team that trusts the numbers.

choices.text: Move English emails to assisted mode now, and keep mixed-language emails in shadow until fixed
choices.outcome: Workable only if English drafts clearly pass 90% on their own and the owner approves the change of scope. It changes the pilot mid-way and needs fresh sign-off.

choices.text: Stop the project: missing the threshold means the idea failed
choices.outcome: The failures are concentrated and fixable. Killing the project throws away a clear path to value.

cards.title: Run a pilot that proves something
cards.prompt: Put the stages of a well-designed pilot in order.
steps: Agree a narrow scope, success criteria and exit rules with the business owner
Run shadow mode: the agent works on real cases, but its outputs are not used
Move to assisted mode: staff see and use outputs at a low autonomy level
Compare results with a similar group working without the agent over the same weeks

cards.title: Real case: a drive-through pilot that was stopped (US, 2024)
cards.body:
From 2021 McDonald's tested automated voice ordering, developed with IBM, in US drive-throughs. In June 2024, after the test had reached more than 100 restaurants, the company told franchisees it would end it by late July 2024. It said it still expected voice ordering to be part of its future and would keep evaluating options. During the test, social media videos of misheard orders drew wide attention.

**Lessons for your pilots:**

- A pilot is a decision tool, not a soft launch. Stopping, or pausing to redesign, is a legitimate result.
- Test in the real, hard conditions: background noise, accents, people changing their minds.
- Agree in advance which results mean scale, redesign or stop, so the decision rests on evidence rather than momentum.
- Customer-facing errors are public: start where staff can catch mistakes before customers see them.

cards.question: A claims-summary pilot ran for six weeks during the summer holiday season, when claim volumes dropped. Pilot teams closed claims 20% faster than in the previous quarter. What is the most reliable way to judge the agent's effect?
options: Compare pilot teams with similar teams without the agent over the same weeks
Compare with the same teams' results from the same months last year
Ask team managers to estimate how much of the gain came from the agent
Accept the 20% as the agent's effect, since staff liked using it
cards.explanation: A comparison group in the same period controls for seasonal swings in volume and case mix. Last year's figures mix in other changes, and opinions are not evidence. Without a comparison, falling volumes could explain the whole gain.

cards.question: The account-opening agent passed every quality threshold in four weeks of shadow mode. What important question can shadow mode NOT answer on its own?
options: Whether its outputs are accurate on real inputs
Whether the live tools respond correctly
How staff behave when they actually rely on its outputs, including over-trusting them
Whether it copes with real customers' language
cards.explanation: Shadow mode tests quality on real inputs and live tools with no customer impact, but because nobody uses the outputs, it cannot show how people work with the agent. That is why an assisted-mode stage follows.

cards.title: Chart Room take-aways
items: Start from painful work and waiting time, and redesign the process rather than automating a broken one.
Good candidates are high-volume, language-heavy, data-accessible, with detectable, reversible errors and known right answers; fixed-rule work suits simple automation.
Score ideas on value, feasibility and risk, and build a portfolio of quick wins and strategic bets, using reuse to break ties.
Honest business cases count running costs and the adoption ramp, and explain how released hours become bankable value.
Data access, quality, documented rules, reliable ground truth and permissions decide success more than model choice.
Pilots need agreed criteria, shadow then assisted mode, a comparison group and exit rules, and the goalposts never move.

cards.prompt: List three candidate agent use cases from your organisation and score each on value, feasibility and risk. Which would you pilot first, and what single success criterion would convince your leadership to scale it?

quiz.question: A process walk of SME loan processing at a Lagos branch shows the credit officer's analysis takes 40 minutes, but files wait an average of six days for a missing document or an approver's signature. What should the team conclude first?
options: An agent that drafts the credit analysis in minutes will remove most of the six-day delay from turnaround time
The best solution is to replace the credit officer with an autonomous agent
AI cannot help with loan processing in any way
Most delay is waiting time, so the hand-offs and document chasing need fixing, not just the analysis
quiz.explanation: Speeding up a 40-minute step barely affects a six-day wait. The big gains lie in redesigning the hand-offs and in chasing documents, where an agent might also help. Replacing the officer ignores the real bottleneck and the risk.

quiz.question: Which process is the weakest candidate for an AI agent?
options: Answering staff questions about current HR policies from an owned, up-to-date policy library
Deciding annual bonuses for senior managers, done once a year with no agreed criteria
Checking vendor invoices against purchase orders, with thousands of invoices a month
Drafting replies to routine customer emails for review
quiz.explanation: Annual senior bonus decisions are rare, high-stakes, sensitive and lack agreed right answers, failing several screening tests at once. The other processes have volume, data and reviewable outputs.

quiz.question: A use case scores Value 5, Feasibility 2, Risk 4 in a prioritisation workshop. How should it be treated?
options: As a strategic bet: plan carefully, close feasibility gaps, start at low autonomy
As a quick win to launch this quarter, because the value score is the highest possible
As a filler to be done if time allows
As a use case to drop permanently
quiz.explanation: High value with low feasibility and high risk is a strategic bet. It is too hard and risky to be a quick win, too valuable to treat as a filler or drop, and suits a cautious, low-autonomy start.

quiz.question: An agent will resolve 40% of a telecom's 20,000 monthly queries end to end, each previously taking 5 minutes of staff time. Loaded staff cost is USD 18 per hour, running costs are USD 4,000 a month and the one-time cost is USD 120,000. What is the simple payback at full run rate?
options: 10 months
30 months
15 months
7.5 months
quiz.explanation: Cases: 20,000 x 40% = 8,000; time: 8,000 x 5 = 40,000 minutes, about 666.7 hours, worth USD 12,000. Net after USD 4,000 running cost is USD 8,000, so payback is USD 120,000 / 8,000 = 15 months. Ten months ignores running costs.

quiz.question: A business case claims USD 1 million annual savings from an agent because it releases 25,000 staff hours a year. The department has no plans to reduce hiring or reassign staff. What is the main weakness?
options: The hourly cost used is probably too low, because it excludes benefits, overheads and supervision costs
Hours are capacity, not cash: no hiring is avoided and no redeployment is planned
Agents cannot realistically release as many as 25,000 hours a year in a single department of this size
Savings should be shown monthly, not annually
quiz.explanation: Hours released are capacity, not cash. Without a plan to avoid hiring, redeploy staff or capture quality benefits, the claimed savings will not appear. The other points do not address this core flaw.

quiz.question: Which item is most often left out of agent business cases, causing benefits to be overstated?
